whatItDoes: Computes the equated monthly installment (EMI) for a fixed-rate loan using the standard reducing-balance formula, and breaks down the full cost of the loan into the monthly EMI, the total amount paid over the term, and the total interest paid. You can adjust the loan amount, annual interest rate, and tenure in years and instantly see how each change affects your payment.
whyItExists: Understanding a loan's full cost is the difference between an affordable purchase and a debt trap. An EMI calculator reveals not just the monthly payment but how much interest compounds over the whole loan life, so borrowers can compare offers on total cost rather than just the headline rate.
whoShouldUse: Home buyers, car buyers, personal-loan borrowers, students comparing education loans, and financial planners estimating loan affordability before committing to a lender.
useCases: Estimate the monthly payment of a home, car, or personal loan before applying
Compare loan offers with different durations and interest rates on total cost
See the total interest paid over the life of a loan to judge whether a shorter term is worth it
Budget a repayment plan that fits your monthly cash flow
Test how a slightly lower rate or shorter tenure changes your monthly burden
Decide between a fixed and floating rate by comparing payments under different rate assumptions
instructions: Enter the total loan amount you plan to borrow
Enter the annual interest rate in percent (e.g., 8.5 for 8.5%)
Read the monthly EMI, total payment, and total interest
Experiment with shorter terms to see how interest shrinks and the EMI rises
Try different rates to compare lenders before you sign
examples: $30,000 at 7% for 5 years → EMI ≈ $594, interest ≈ $5,650, total ≈ $35,650
Same $200,000 loan at 8.5% for 15 years → EMI ≈ $1,969, but interest drops to ≈ $154,500 — a saving of ≈ $62,000 in interest
bestPractices: Compare the total interest cost, not just the monthly EMIs, when choosing a term
Try shorter tenures to reduce total interest when you can afford a higher EMI
Include processing fees, documentation charges, and insurance separately in your total-cost estimate
Re-check the rate with the lender, since advertised rates change and often differ from the final offer
Keep a small buffer in your budget — EMIs above ~40% of net income strain most households
commonMistakes: Comparing loans only on their interest rates while ignoring tenure and total cost
Entering the rate as 0.085 instead of 8.5, which produces a wildly wrong EMI
Forgetting that processing fees and insurance premiums are not included in the EMI
Assuming the EMI amount stays constant forever on a variable-rate loan
Extending tenure just to lower the EMI without noticing the extra lakhs of interest it adds
faq: What is the EMI formula? — It is the standard reducing-balance annuity: principal × monthly rate × (1+rate)^n / ((1+rate)^n − 1).
Does it include processing fees or insurance? — No, only principal and interest. Add fees separately for a true total cost.
Can I use it for any loan type? — Yes, the math is identical for home, auto, and personal loans; only the rates differ.
Is my data sent anywhere? — No, the calculation happens entirely in your browser.
How is the reducing balance different from simple interest? — With a reducing balance you pay interest only on the remaining principal, so the interest share of each EMI shrinks over time.
Should I pick a longer or shorter tenure? — Shorter tenures mean higher EMIs but much less total interest; longer tenures lower the EMI but multiply total interest.
